summary: Clarifies how explicit tracking works in Multicast VPN (MVPN), the procedure by which a multicast ingress node learns which egress nodes want a given flow. The base MVPN specifications (RFC 6513 and RFC 6514) were unclear in some scenarios. This document fills those gaps and defines a new way to handle wildcard routes. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8534 sharpens how a multicast VPN router finds out who wants the traffic it is carrying. It adds a new flag that says 'tell me about each flow separately', so one router can send a single request and get back an answer naming every flow and every interested router, rather than a list of interested routers only.

subtitle: How a multicast ingress router learns which egress routers want each flow, with a single wildcard request.

tldr.problem: In a multicast VPN, the router that receives a customer's multicast traffic has to know which other routers want that traffic, and the base specifications left gaps when a wildcard route was used.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Leaf Information Required per Flow flag to the PMSI Tunnel attribute, so a single wildcard route can ask every egress router to answer with one Leaf A-D route per individual flow it wants.
tldr.outcome: An ingress node can now learn exactly which egress node wants which flow, instead of only learning which egress nodes want some flow from it, and it does so with one advertisement rather than one per flow.

facts.label: Places the flag may be set
facts.value: Wildcard S-PMSI A-D and Leaf A-D routes

today: RFC 8534 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates the multicast VPN specifications RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, and it registers the Leaf Information Required per-Flow flag with the value 2 in the PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags registry.

sections.title: The Problem With Wildcard Routes
sections.content:
The base Multicast VPN specifications, RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, define the Selective Provider Multicast Service Interface Auto-Discovery route, the S-PMSI A-D route. Its Network Layer Reachability Information field identifies a particular multicast flow, denoted by a pair of addresses: C-S, the IP source address, and C-G, the IP multicast address, both in the address space of a VPN customer. The route also carries a PMSI Tunnel attribute, typically used to identify a tunnel through the provider backbone, a P-tunnel. Originating such a route says that if the node has to transmit packets of the identified flow over the backbone, it will send them through the identified tunnel.

The same specifications define a procedure that lets the ingress node of a flow determine the set of egress nodes that have asked to receive that flow from it. That ability is called explicit tracking. The ingress node requests it by setting the Leaf Information Required flag, the LIR flag, in the PMSI Tunnel attribute. An egress node that receives an S-PMSI A-D route with the LIR flag set originates a Leaf A-D route whose NLRI contains the NLRI of the S-PMSI A-D route, advertising that it wants to receive that particular flow.

RFC 6625 extends the S-PMSI A-D route so that the source address, the group address or both can be replaced by wildcards, giving wildcard S-PMSI A-D routes. One purpose of RFC 8534 is to clarify how explicit tracking applies when wildcard routes are used.

The document also addresses a case the earlier specifications do not. Suppose the ingress node originates a (C-*,C-*) wildcard route that identifies a P-tunnel, and wants explicit tracking for each individual flow it transmits on that tunnel. If it sets only the LIR flag, each egress node answers with a Leaf A-D route carrying the (C-*,C-*) wildcard, which tells the ingress node which egress nodes want flows from it but not which flow each of them wants. To learn that, the ingress node has to originate an S-PMSI A-D route for every individual flow, with the LIR flag set in each, and since the tunnel is already fixed by the wildcard route, each of those routes can carry 'no tunnel information present'.

That works but needs clarifications, and it is not the most efficient form. It would be better if the ingress node could send a single wildcard route binding the set of flows to a tunnel and have the egress nodes answer with a Leaf A-D route for each individual flow. The RFC also addresses segmentation, where a P-tunnel passes through a number of segmentation domains, each with its own ingress node and set of egress nodes: the explicit tracking procedures do not let an ingress node see past the boundary of its domain, and the earlier specifications are unclear about whether a segmented tunnel egress node forwards an S-PMSI A-D route whose PTA says 'no tunnel information present' to the next domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router at the edge of a provider network advertises which customer multicast flows it wants. The router that receives the customer's traffic has to collect those answers to know where to send it. When a single advertisement covers many flows at once, the answers come back aggregated, and the sender learns who is interested but not in which flow. This RFC adds a way to get the finer answer without asking about every flow separately.

sections.title: The Two Tracking Flags
sections.content:
RFC 6514 defines one flag in the PMSI Tunnel attribute, the Leaf Information Required flag, used for explicit tracking. This document defines a new flag in the Flags field of the same attribute, the Leaf Information Required per Flow flag, LIR-pF.

The LIR-pF flag may be set in the PTA of a (C-*,C-*), (C-*,C-G) or (C-S,C-*) wildcard S-PMSI A-D route, and it may also be set in the PTA of a Leaf A-D route. The flag is only defined for those cases; in all other cases it should be clear and its value should be ignored.

Support for the LIR-pF flag is optional. The flag should not be set in a route's PTA unless it is known that the flag is supported by all the Provider Edge routers that are to receive that route. Typically this means an operator would control the ability to set the flag with a configuration knob, and would not turn it on unless all the relevant routers support it.

If the LIR-pF flag is set in the PTA of an S-PMSI A-D route, the originator must also set the LIR flag. If the PTA of a received wildcard S-PMSI A-D route has LIR-pF set but not LIR, the receiver must log that the flags appear to have been set improperly, but must then process the route normally, as if both flags were set.

The RFC also limits itself to the tunnel types listed in Section 5 of RFC 6514, which it calls 6514-tunnel-types. Other tunnel types need their own specification to say how the LIR-pF flag is used with them. Until such a specification exists, the originator of a route should not set the flag in a PTA naming such a tunnel type, and the receiver should treat the flag as if it were not set.

If the flag is set but some egress nodes do not support it, two things follow. The ingress node cannot determine the complete set of egress nodes expecting a particular flow, and, depending on the tunnel type, it may send a flow only to the egress nodes that do support the flag, so that from the point of view of the others some flows appear to be blackholed. The ingress node can detect the problem: an egress node that does not support the flag answers with a Leaf A-D route whose PTA lacks the flag, and the software at the ingress node must detect this and must be able to alert the operator that the deployment is not properly configured.

IANA has registered the new flag with the value 2 in the PMSI Tunnel Attribute Flags registry.
sections.plainLanguage: There are now two flags in the tunnel attribute. The older one asks the receiver to answer at all. The new one asks for an answer per flow. The new flag is optional in a router, so an operator should only turn it on where every router understands it, and the ingress node can spot a router that does not and warn about it.

sections.title: Match for Tracking versus Match for Reception
sections.content:
Section 3.2 of RFC 6625 gives rules for finding the S-PMSI A-D route that is the match for data reception of a given state. Those rules did not take into account routes that carry no PTA at all, or a PTA that identifies no P-tunnel. This RFC modifies them: it is required to ignore any S-PMSI A-D route that has no PTA, or whose PTA specifies 'no tunnel information present'. The same requirement applies to the modified rules in other documents such as RFC 7582 and RFC 7900.

The RFC then introduces a new notion, the match for tracking. For a given flow, the match for tracking is chosen by ignoring any S-PMSI A-D route that has no PTA, and ignoring any S-PMSI A-D route whose PTA says 'no tunnel information present' and has neither the LIR flag nor the LIR-pF flag set. In other words such a route is ignored only when both flags are clear. The rules for finding the match for reception are then applied, and the result, if any, is the match for tracking.

The RFC works through examples. Suppose PE1 has chosen PE2 as the upstream PE for the flow (C-S1,C-G1) and has installed two routes originated by PE2: Route1, a (C-*,C-*) S-PMSI A-D route whose PTA specifies a tunnel, and Route2, a (C-S1,C-G1) S-PMSI A-D route whose PTA says 'no tunnel information present' and has the LIR flag set. Route1 is the match for reception and Route2 is the match for tracking. If PE1 has instead chosen PE2 as upstream for a different flow (C-S2,C-G2) and PE2 has not originated a route for it, then Route1 is the match for tracking for that flow as well as the match for reception.

If a match for tracking has neither the LIR flag nor the LIR-pF flag set, no explicit tracking information is generated. In another example, where Route1 is a (C-*,C-*) route and Route2 is a (C-S1,C-G1) route whose PTA specifies a tunnel, Route2 is both the match for reception and the match for tracking. The match for reception can be the same route as the match for tracking, or a less specific one, but it can never be more specific.
sections.plainLanguage: A router works out two different things about the routes it has been sent: which route says where the traffic should actually go, and which route is the one to answer. The two are usually the same. They differ when the route that names the tunnel is a broad one and a narrower route was sent just to ask for tracking. The RFC spells out how to pick each one.

sections.title: How an Ingress Node Starts Tracking
sections.content:
An ingress node that needs explicit tracking for a flow or a set of flows can use one of two procedures.

The first is to originate an S-PMSI A-D route that identifies the flow in its NLRI, including a PTA, and set the LIR flag in that PTA. The PTA may specify a particular tunnel or 'no tunnel information present'. However, the PTA of such a route should not say 'no tunnel information present' unless the ingress node also originates a route carrying a PTA that specifies the tunnel to be used for the traffic, which could be an Inclusive Provider Multicast Service Interface Auto-Discovery route, a (C-*,C-G1) route, a (C-S1,C-*) route or a (C-*,C-*) route. There is no point in requesting explicit tracking for a flow that is not being carried on any tunnel.

If the ingress node originates a wildcard S-PMSI A-D route carrying the PTA that specifies the tunnel, and that PTA has the LIR-pF flag set, then explicit tracking for the flow is requested by that wildcard route, and the ingress node should not originate a separate (C-S1,C-G1) route with 'no tunnel information present', since it would add nothing.

Tracking that was started by a route whose PTA says 'no tunnel information present' is terminated by withdrawing the route. Tracking that was started by a route whose PTA specifies a tunnel is terminated by re-originating the route with the LIR flag cleared.

The second procedure may be used only when it is known that the egress nodes support the optional LIR-pF flag. The ingress node originates a wildcard S-PMSI A-D route and sets the LIR-pF flag in its PTA, and the egress nodes that need any of the flows matching that wildcard each originate a Leaf A-D route for the flows they want. The PTA of the wildcard route may specify a tunnel or 'no tunnel information present'; the choice is outside the scope of the document. Tracking started this way is terminated by withdrawing the route, or, when the PTA specifies a tunnel, by re-originating the route with both the LIR and LIR-pF flags cleared.

This second procedure may not give the expected results if some egress nodes do not support the LIR-pF flag, so it should not be used in that case.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to ask. The older way asks about one flow at a time. The newer way asks with a single broad route and asks the receivers to answer per flow, but it only works if every receiver understands the new flag. Both ways are undone in the same style, either by withdrawing the route or by sending it again with the flag turned off.

sections.title: How an Egress Node Answers
sections.content:
To respond to a match for tracking that has the LIR-pF flag set, an egress node originates one or more Leaf A-D routes. If the node has multicast state for a flow and has determined that a particular S-PMSI A-D route with the flag set is the match for tracking for that flow, then, if the node supports the flag, it must originate a Leaf A-D route whose NLRI identifies that particular flow. If a single wildcard S-PMSI A-D route is the match for tracking for several flows, the egress node may need to originate several Leaf A-D routes, one for each such flow.

The NLRI of each such Leaf A-D route is built from the fields shown in the RFC's Figure 1: the Route Distinguisher, the Multicast Source Length, the Multicast Source, the Multicast Group Length, the Multicast Group and the ingress PE's IP address. The ingress PE address is taken from the Originating Router field of the match for tracking. The source and group fields together identify the flow being tracked; if a (C-*,C-G) is being tracked the Multicast Source field is omitted and its length is set to 0, which makes the route a wildcard Leaf A-D route. The Route Distinguisher is copied from the NLRI of the match for tracking.

Because the RD in these routes is never 0 or -1, they can always be told apart from the Leaf A-D routes constructed for global table multicast, and they are VPN-specific routes that always carry an IP-address-specific Route Target.

If the Leaf A-D route is originated in response to a match for tracking whose PTA says 'no tunnel information present', the Leaf A-D route must carry a PTA that says 'no tunnel information present' with the LIR-pF flag set. If an egress node originates several Leaf A-D routes in response to a single S-PMSI A-D route, and that route is later withdrawn, the Leaf A-D routes must also be withdrawn. A Leaf A-D route also needs to be withdrawn if the egress node changes its upstream multicast hop for the flow, or no longer needs that flow.

For the tunnel types listed in RFC 6514 there are two extra rules. If the tunnel type of the match for tracking or reception is Ingress Replication, the Leaf A-D route's PTA may specify Ingress Replication, in which case the MPLS label field may be a non-zero value, and that label will be used by the ingress PE when it transmits to the egress PE the packets of the flow identified in the Leaf A-D route's NLRI. The egress PE may instead specify a label of zero, or specify 'no tunnel information present', in which case the ingress PE uses the label the egress PE gave in the PTA of the Leaf A-D route it originated in response to the LIR flag of the match for reception. For any other 6514 tunnel type, the PTA attached to the Leaf A-D route must specify 'no tunnel information present'.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver answers with one route per flow it wants, each naming the flow exactly. The reply carries the flag so that the sender knows the answer is the detailed kind. If the reply names a label, the sender uses that label when it sends the traffic; otherwise it keeps using the label it already had.

sections.title: When the Egress Node Is a Border Router
sections.content:
When segmented P-tunnels are used, the ingress and egress nodes may be Area Border Routers or Autonomous System Border Routers. An egress ABR or ASBR that receives and installs an S-PMSI A-D route also forwards that route. If the received PTA specifies a tunnel, the egress ABR or ASBR may change the PTA before forwarding the route in order to specify a different tunnel type.

If the received route has a PTA specifying a tunnel and the LIR-pF flag set, the egress ABR or ASBR originates a corresponding Leaf A-D route for a given flow only if it knows it needs to receive that flow, which it knows by having received a corresponding Leaf A-D route from downstream.

The rest of the section applies only when the egress ABR or ASBR has installed an S-PMSI A-D route whose PTA says 'no tunnel information present' but has the LIR flag or the LIR-pF flag set. In that case the PTA must be passed along unchanged when the route is forwarded: a PTA saying 'no tunnel information present' must not be changed into one specifying a tunnel, and the LIR and LIR-pF flags must be passed along unchanged.

Propagating such a route may cause the egress ABR or ASBR to receive Leaf A-D routes that correspond to it, carrying an IP-address-specific Route Target that names the egress ABR or ASBR. It propagates those Leaf A-D routes after changing the Route Target, setting the Global Administrator field to the IP address taken from the S-PMSI A-D route's Next-Hop field or from its Segmented Point-to-Multipoint Next-Hop Extended Community, preferring the Extended Community when it is present.

This lets the ingress PE explicitly track the egress PEs for a given flow even when segmented tunnels are used. However, cross-domain explicit tracking uses S-PMSI A-D routes that do not specify tunnel information, so it can only be done when the S-PMSI A-D route that is a flow's match for tracking is different from the one that is its match for reception.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel can be split into segments at the borders between areas or autonomous systems, and the question of who wants a flow has to be answered across those boundaries. The rule is that the tracking request has to be passed on unchanged, and the answers that come back have to be re-tagged with the address of the border router that received them.

sections.title: What the Ingress Node Does With the Answer
sections.content:
Consider an ingress node N that receives a Leaf A-D route L, where L carries an IP-address-specific Route Target identifying N, and the Route Key field of L's NLRI is not identical to the NLRI of any current I-PMSI or S-PMSI A-D route originated by N. Under the procedures of RFC 6514 and RFC 7524 such a Leaf A-D route causes no MVPN-specific action to be taken by N.

This document changes that in one case: there is a current wildcard S-PMSI A-D route, originated by N, to which L is a valid response under the procedures of Section 5.2. In that case L must be processed by N.

If L's PTA specifies a tunnel type of Ingress Replication and a non-zero MPLS label, then when N needs to send L a packet belonging to the multicast flow or flows identified in L's NLRI, N must use the specified label. If L's PTA says 'no tunnel information present', or specifies Ingress Replication with an MPLS label of zero, or specifies any other 6514 tunnel type, then what N does with L is a local matter. The Leaf A-D route gives N explicit tracking information for the flow, but that information is for management and monitoring and has no direct effect on the flow of multicast traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally an answer that matches no advertisement the ingress node made is ignored. The exception is an answer to a broad request: then it is used. If the answer carries a label, the ingress node must use that label when it sends the traffic; otherwise the answer is used for reporting only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 apply.

By setting the LIR-pF flag in a single wildcard S-PMSI A-D route, a large number of Leaf A-D routes can be elicited. If the flag is set when it is not wanted, through error or malfeasance, a significant increase in control plane overhead can result. Properly protecting the control plane should prevent this kind of attack.

Mitigating such an attack is unfortunately not straightforward. The ingress node can notice that it is receiving, in response to an S-PMSI A-D route whose LIR-pF flag is clear, Leaf A-D routes that have the flag set, and by default the reception of such a route must be logged. Because such log entries can be false positives that generate a lot of noise, implementations should have a knob to disable this logging.

Withdrawing the S-PMSI A-D route would in theory stop the attack, but it is not a good strategy in practice. Under normal operating conditions there are race conditions that may make the ingress node think it is being attacked when it is not. If some egress nodes have a bug that causes them to set the flag when it should be clear, withdrawing the route stops the flow of multicast data to all the egress nodes, causing an unnecessary customer-visible disruption. And the situation that caused the route to be originated in the first place will still exist after the withdrawal, so the route will just be re-originated.

The conclusion is that any action that would ameliorate the effects of this attack would likely have a negative effect during normal operation, so it is better to rely on the security mechanisms that protect the control plane generally.
sections.plainLanguage: The new flag can be used to make a router generate a flood of replies. The RFC explains why it does not add a special defence: any targeted response would also break normal operation, so the answer is to protect the control plane in general rather than to add a rule for this one case.

items.text: The flag is defined for wildcard S-PMSI A-D routes and for Leaf A-D routes; elsewhere it should be clear.
